title: Predicting Heart Disease Risk: Logistic Regression vs. Random Forest
text:
Can patient health data, such as blood pressure, cholesterol, BMI, smoking status, exercise habits, and 15 other features, predict whether someone has heart disease?
Data: Heart Disease Risk dataset (10,000 patient records, 21 columns, binary target Heart Disease Status).
Two models are compared using an identical preprocessing pipeline, for a fair comparison:

Logistic Regression (glm): a linear baseline
Random Forest (ranger, 500 trees): can capture non-linear patterns and feature interactions that logistic regression structurally cannot



Code
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(ranger)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

Missingness


Code
colSums(is.na(heart))


                 Age               Gender       Blood Pressure 
                  29                   19                   19 
   Cholesterol Level      Exercise Habits              Smoking 
                  30                   25                   25 
Family Heart Disease             Diabetes                  BMI 
                  21                   30                   22 
 High Blood Pressure  Low HDL Cholesterol High LDL Cholesterol 
                  26                   25                   26

                  32                   22                   25 
   Sugar Consumption   Triglyceride Level  Fasting Blood Sugar 
                  30                   26                   22 
           CRP Level   Homocysteine Level Heart Disease Status 
                  26                   20                    0 


Every column has only light, scattered missingness (roughly 0.2–0.3% of rows each). With nothing standing out as a heavily-missing column, the simplest defensible approach is listwise deletion, drop any row with at least one missing value, rather than building per-column imputation logic that would add complexity without meaningfully changing the results.


Code
heart_clean <- heart %>% drop_na()

nrow(heart)


[1] 10000


Code
nrow(heart_clean)


[1] 9500


This drops about 5% of rows (10,000 → 9,500), a reasonable trade-off for guaranteeing a fully complete dataset.


Class Balance


Code
heart_clean %>% count(`Heart Disease Status`) %>% mutate(pct = n / sum(n))


# A tibble: 2 × 3
  `Heart Disease Status`     n   pct
  <chr>                  <int> <dbl>
1 No                      7597 0.800
2 Yes                     1903 0.200


The target is imbalanced: ~80% No / ~20% Yes. This one fact drives several downstream decisions:

A model that always predicts “No” already scores 80% accuracy while being clinically useless, so accuracy alone is not a trustworthy metric.
The train/test split must be stratified on this column to preserve the ratio in both sets.
Sensitivity (catching actual positive cases) matters more than raw accuracy in a health-screening context, since a false negative (telling a sick patient they’re fine) is the costlier mistake.

3. Train/Test Split & Preprocessing


Code
set.seed(42)

split <- initial_split(heart_clean, prop = 0.8, strata = `Heart Disease Status`)
train_data <- training(split)
test_data  <- testing(split)

nrow(train_data)


[1] 7599


Code
nrow(test_data)


[1] 1901




Code
heart_recipe <- recipe(`Heart Disease Status` ~ ., data = train_data) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

heart_recipe


One shared recipe feeds both models below, so any performance difference between them reflects the model, not inconsistent preprocessing.

text:
6. Model Comparison


Code
model_comparison <- bind_rows(
  class_metrics(results, truth = `Heart Disease Status`, estimate = .pred_class, event_level = "second") %>%
    mutate(model = "Logistic Regression"),
  class_metrics(rf_results, truth = `Heart Disease Status`, estimate = .pred_class, event_level = "second") %>%
    mutate(model = "Random Forest")
) %>%
  bind_rows(
    roc_auc(results, truth = `Heart Disease Status`, .pred_Yes, event_level = "second") %>% mutate(model = "Logistic Regression"),
    roc_auc(rf_results, truth = `Heart Disease Status`, .pred_Yes, event_level = "second") %>% mutate(model = "Random Forest")
  ) %>%
  select(model, .metric, .estimate) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = .estimate)

model_comparison

title: Predicting Heart Disease Risk: Logistic Regression vs. Random Forest
text:
7. Results & Conclusion
Both models converge on the same result:








Metric
Logistic Regression
Random Forest




Accuracy
0.800
0.800


Sensitivity
0.000
0.000


Specificity
1.000
1.000


Precision
NA (no positive predictions made)
NA (no positive predictions made)


ROC AUC
0.476
0.477



Headline finding: neither model found usable signal in these features. Both an AUC of ~0.48 (versus 0.5 for a coin flip) and a confusion matrix where every single test-set prediction was “No” point to the same conclusion that at the default 50% classification threshold, the model has learned that predicting the majority class is the safest bet, because none of the 20 predictors (age, blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking, exercise habits, etc.) are informative enough on their own to justify ever predicting “Yes.”
This is not a coding error or a modeling mistake and it’s confirmed by two structurally different model types landing on the same result. Logistic regression can only detect linear relationships; random forest can detect non-linear patterns and feature interactions. Agreement between them is stronger evidence of “no signal in the data” than either model failing alone would be.
Why this matters for interpreting the dataset: datasets like this are sometimes synthetically generated for practice purposes, which can mean the relationship between features and outcome is intentionally weak or randomized rather than reflecting real clinical patterns. Reporting a null result clearly rather than tuning parameters until a misleadingly optimistic number appears is the more defensible, more useful analysis.
What I’d try next: - Lower the classification threshold well below 50% (e.g. flag “Yes” at >20% predicted probability) to explore the sensitivity/specificity tradeoff directly, even though it won’t change the underlying AUC. - Check feature-target correlations individually before modeling, to catch a signal-free dataset earlier in the process. - If treating this as a real screening tool, prioritize collecting features with known clinical predictive value (family history detail, actual lab panels, prior cardiac events) over adding more model complexity.

Data source: Heart Disease Risk dataset, Kaggle.

title: Database Querying with SQL (MS Access)
text: A relational database (employees, departments, members, products, transactions, and classes) built across class coursework covering filtering, aggregation, joins, and layered/subqueries. All queries below are copied directly from Access’s SQL View (not reconstructed), so the syntax reflects exactly what runs against the database.

title: Database Querying with SQL (MS Access)
text: A relational database (employees, departments, members, products, transactions, and classes) built across class coursework covering filtering, aggregation, joins, and layered/subqueries. All queries below are copied directly from Access’s SQL View (not reconstructed), so the syntax reflects exactly what runs against the database.

title: Database Querying with SQL (MS Access)
text:
2. Filtering with WHERE
Pattern matching with a positional wildcard (S followed by exactly four characters), combined with multiple conditions and a NULL check to exclude former employees:
SELECT
    tblEmployee.EmpFirst,
    tblEmployee.EmpLast,
    tblEmployee.JobTitle,
    tblEmployee.Salary
FROM
    tblEmployee
WHERE
    (
        ((tblEmployee.EmpFirst) LIKE "S????")
        AND ((tblEmployee.EmpEndDate) IS NULL)
        AND ((tblEmployee.IsFullTime) = Yes)
    )
ORDER BY
    tblEmployee.Salary DESC;
Date-range filtering with BETWEEN, combined with OR logic across two states:
SELECT
    tblEmployee.EmpFirst,
    tblEmployee.EmpLast,
    tblEmployee.EmpPhone,
    tblEmployee.EmpStartDate
FROM
    tblEmployee
WHERE
    (
        (
            (tblEmployee.EmpState) = "OK"
            OR (tblEmployee.EmpState) = "IL"
        )
        AND (
            (tblEmployee.EmpStartDate) BETWEEN #1/1/2017# AND #12/31/2019#
        )
    )
ORDER BY
    tblEmployee.EmpLast;

title: Database Querying with SQL (MS Access)
text:
3. Aggregate Functions
Summary statistics across a filtered subset (part-time employees hired before 2015), no grouping included here since the result is a single row:
SELECT
    Max(tblEmployee.[HourlyRate]) AS HourlyMax,
    Min(tblEmployee.[HourlyRate]) AS HourlyMin,
    Avg(tblEmployee.[HourlyRate]) AS HourlyAvg
FROM
    tblEmployee
WHERE
    (
        ((tblEmployee.IsFullTime) = No)
        AND ((tblEmployee.EmpEndDate) IS NULL)
        AND ((tblEmployee.EmpStartDate) < #1/1/2015#)
    );

title: Database Querying with SQL (MS Access)
text:
4. GROUP BY with JOIN
Total salary cost per department; an explicit INNER JOIN linking two tables on their shared key, then GROUP BY to roll salaries up by department:
SELECT
    tblEmpDepartment.EmpDepartmentName,
    Sum(tblEmployee.[Salary]) AS TotalSalaries
FROM
    tblEmpDepartment
    INNER JOIN tblEmployee ON tblEmpDepartment.EmpDepartmentID = tblEmployee.EmpDepartmentID
WHERE
    (
        ((tblEmployee.IsFullTime) = Yes)
        AND ((tblEmployee.EmpEndDate) IS NULL)
    )
GROUP BY
    tblEmpDepartment.EmpDepartmentName
ORDER BY
    Sum(tblEmployee.[Salary]) DESC;

title: Database Querying with SQL (MS Access)
section: 5. GROUP BY with HAVING, Calculated Fields, and Multi-Table Joins
text:
5. GROUP BY with HAVING, Calculated Fields, and Multi-Table Joins
The most involved query in the set: revenue and commission per employee, computed from a calculated field (Quantity × SellingPrice × (1 - Discount)), joined across four tables, grouped by employee, and then filtered on the aggregated result itself using HAVING — showing employees whose total revenue hit $5,000+, something a WHERE clause can’t do since WHERE filters rows before aggregation, not after:
SELECT
    tblEmployee.EmployeeID,
    [EmpLast] & ", " & [EmpFirst] AS Name,
    Sum(
        (
            [Quantity] * [SellingPrice] * (1 - [ProductDiscount])
        )
    ) AS Revenue,
    Sum(
        (
            [Quantity] * [SellingPrice] * (1 - [ProductDiscount])
        ) * 0.05
    ) AS CommissionAmt
FROM
    (
        tblEmployee
        INNER JOIN tblTransaction ON tblEmployee.EmployeeID = tblTransaction.ProcessedBy
    )
    INNER JOIN (
        tblProduct
        INNER JOIN tblProductInTransaction ON tblProduct.ProductID = tblProductInTransaction.ProductID
    ) ON tblTransaction.TransactionID = tblProductInTransaction.TransactionID
WHERE
    (
        ((tblTransaction.TransactionLocation) <> "Online")
        AND (
            (tblTransaction.TransactionDate) BETWEEN #1/1/2024# AND #10/31/2024#
        )
        AND ((tblEmployee.EmpEndDate) IS NULL)
    )
GROUP BY
    tblEmployee.EmployeeID,
    [EmpLast] & ", " & [EmpFirst]
HAVING
    (
        (
            Sum(
                (
                    [Quantity] * [SellingPrice] * (1 - [ProductDiscount])
                )
            )
        ) >= 5000
    )
ORDER BY
    [EmpLast] & ", " & [EmpFirst];

title: Database Querying with SQL (MS Access)
text:
6. Conditional Logic
IIf(), which is Access’s equivalent of SQL Server’s CASE WHEN, used to derive a Yes/No flag from an existing field rather than storing it redundantly:
SELECT
    tblEmployee.EmployeeID,
    tblEmployee.EmpFirst,
    tblEmployee.EmpLast,
    tblEmployee.JobTitle,
    IIf([JobTitle] = 1, "Yes", "No") AS BonusEligible
FROM
    tblEmployee
WHERE
    (
        ((tblEmployee.IsFullTime) = Yes)
        AND ((tblEmployee.EmpEndDate) IS NULL)
    )
ORDER BY
    tblEmployee.EmployeeID,
    tblEmployee.EmpLast;

title: Database Querying with SQL (MS Access)
text:
7. Layered Queries (Subquery Pattern)
Access’s query designer doesn’t support inline subqueries as cleanly as full SQL Server, so the standard workaround and the pattern used throughout this database is to save intermediate results as their own queries, then reference those saved queries the same way you’d reference a table.
Goal: find what percentage of all class enrollments each class represents.
Query 1 — total enrollment across all classes (the denominator):
SELECT
    Count(tblEmployeeInClass.EmployeeID) AS TotalEnrollment
FROM
    tblEmployeeInClass;
Query 2 — enrollment per class (the numerator), grouped with a join:
SELECT
    tblClass.ClassName,
    Count(tblEmployeeInClass.EmployeeID) AS ClassEnrollment
FROM
    tblClass
    INNER JOIN tblEmployeeInClass ON tblClass.ClassID = tblEmployeeInClass.ClassID
GROUP BY
    tblClass.ClassName;
Query 3 — divides one saved query by the other to get the final percentage:
SELECT
    [qryCH09-DIS03_Numerator].ClassName,
    [ClassEnrollment] / [TotalEnrollment] AS PercentOfEnrollment
FROM
    [qryCH09-DIS03_Numerator],
    [qryCH09-DIS03_Denominator]
ORDER BY
    [ClassEnrollment] / [TotalEnrollment] DESC;
Second example of the same pattern — identifying members who spent above the average in Q4 2024. This is functionally equivalent to a correlated subquery with HAVING SUM(...) > (SELECT AVG(...)) in full SQL, decomposed into three linked steps:
Query 1 — total spend per member in Q4:
SELECT
    tblMember.MemberID,
    tblMember.MemberFirstN,
    tblMember.MemberLastN,
    tblMember.MemberEmail,
    Sum(
        [Quantity] * [SellingPrice] * (1 - [ProductDiscount])
    ) AS TotalSpent
FROM
    (
        tblMember
        INNER JOIN tblTransaction ON tblMember.MemberID = tblTransaction.MemberID
    )
    INNER JOIN (
        tblProduct
        INNER JOIN tblProductInTransaction ON tblProduct.ProductID = tblProductInTransaction.ProductID
    ) ON tblTransaction.TransactionID = tblProductInTransaction.TransactionID
WHERE
    (
        (tblTransaction.TransactionDate) BETWEEN #10/1/2024# AND #12/31/2024#
    )
GROUP BY
    tblMember.MemberID,
    tblMember.MemberFirstN,
    tblMember.MemberLastN,
    tblMember.MemberEmail;
Query 2 — the average of that result:
SELECT
    Avg([qryCH09-CAS01-Q4AmtSpent].TotalSpent) AS AvgOfTotalSpent
FROM
    [qryCH09-CAS01-Q4AmtSpent];
Query 3 — members whose spend exceeds that average:
SELECT
    [qryCH09-CAS01-Q4AmtSpent].MemberID,
    [qryCH09-CAS01-Q4AmtSpent].MemberFirstN,
    [qryCH09-CAS01-Q4AmtSpent].MemberLastN,
    [qryCH09-CAS01-Q4AmtSpent].MemberEmail,
    [qryCH09-CAS01-Q4AmtSpent].TotalSpent
FROM
    [qryCH09-CAS01-AverageSpent],
    [qryCH09-CAS01-Q4AmtSpent]
WHERE
    (
        ([qryCH09-CAS01-Q4AmtSpent].TotalSpent) > [AvgOfTotalSpent]
    );

title: Database Querying with SQL (MS Access)
text:
8. Skills Summary

Filtering: WHERE, wildcard LIKE, BETWEEN, IS NULL, compound AND/OR logic
Aggregation: SUM, AVG, COUNT, MAX, MIN, with and without GROUP BY
Filtering on aggregates specifically with HAVING (distinct from filtering rows with WHERE)
Multi-table INNER JOIN, including joins nested across more than two tables
Calculated fields (arithmetic and string concatenation in SELECT)
Conditional logic with IIf()
Query decomposition — building layered queries to simulate subqueries

title: Cleaning Corrupted POS Data in Excel
text:
1. Problem Statement
A local coffee shop’s point-of-sale system presented with corrupted characters, malformed dates, and inconsistent formatting into one week of transaction data. The task: rebuild a dynamic cleaning process that could take a fresh batch of corrupted data pasted into the same columns and re-clean it automatically, without manually rewriting formulas each time. Then, run exploratory analysis on the recovered data.
Three fields needed cleaning: Date, Item, and PricePoint. All formulas below are live Excel formulas, not one-time manual fixes.

title: Cleaning Corrupted POS Data in Excel
text:
2. Date Repair
Dates arrived as inconsistent text strings like "2025++5/25" instead of real Excel dates.
=TEXTSPLIT(B2,{"++","/"})
Splits the raw string on two different delimiters at once (++ and /) into separate year/month/day pieces with the TEXTSPLIT function that handles multiple delimiters in one call, instead of nesting several LEFT/MID/FIND formulas.
=DATE(J2,K2,L2)
=IF(M2=9999,"???",M2)
Reconstructs a real date from the split parts, then flags unrecoverable rows with ??? instead of a broken value — so downstream analysis never silently includes garbage.

Before → After



Transaction ID
Raw Date
Cleaned Date




427999
2025++5/25
5/25/2025


428002
1927++5/17
???



That second row exposes a genuine bug, verified against the workbook’s own computed values — and it’s more interesting than a simple missed edge case. DATE(1927, 5, 17) doesn’t fail to parse; it correctly returns a valid date serial number. The problem is that this particular date’s serial number is exactly 9999 — the same value chosen as the sentinel for “this date is invalid.” So a perfectly legitimate (if suspiciously old) date gets wrongly flagged as broken, precisely because the sentinel value wasn’t actually impossible to collide with. This is a real, well-known category of bug in data engineering — picking a “magic value” to mean missing/invalid without confirming it can never occur naturally in the data. A more robust fix would use a value clearly outside any valid date serial range (e.g., a negative number, or a dedicated boolean flag column) instead of overloading a plausible date value as the error signal.

title: Cleaning Corrupted POS Data in Excel
text:
3. Item Name Repair
Item names had corrupted encoding artifacts (©, ☐, §) injected in place of spaces.
=SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(D2,"©"," "),"☐"," "),"§"," ")
=PROPER(TRIM(CLEAN(P2)))
Nested SUBSTITUTE() calls strip each corrupted character in turn, then CLEAN() removes any remaining non-printable characters, TRIM() collapses extra whitespace, and PROPER() normalizes capitalization — a standard three-function stack for text normalization.

title: Cleaning Corrupted POS Data in Excel
text:
4. Price Point Standardization
=SUBSTITUTE(E2,"ounce","oz")
Standardizes unit labeling so it matches the format used in the shop’s existing price list (e.g., "12 ounce" → "12 oz"), keeping the cleaned data consistent with everything already on file.

title: Cleaning Corrupted POS Data in Excel
text:
5. Exploratory Analysis
Once the data was clean, I built a lookup key and ran revenue analysis:
=CONCAT(D2,F2)
=E2*XLOOKUP(L2,PriceListData!$F$2:$F$97,PriceListData!$E$2:$E$97)
CONCAT builds a composite key (Item + Price Point, e.g. "Cappuccino12 oz") so each specific size/variant of a product can be matched to its correct price via XLOOKUP — the modern, more flexible successor to VLOOKUP (it can look left or right, and returns a clear result instead of #N/A when paired with its if_not_found argument).
=UNIQUE(TransactionData!A2:A7396)
=SUMIF(TransactionData!$A$2:$A$7396, O2, TransactionData!$M$2:$M$7396)
UNIQUE deduplicates transaction IDs (a single purchase can span multiple rows if several items were bought together), and SUMIF rolls up total revenue per transaction.
From there, I computed a full descriptive statistics summary including mean, median, standard deviation, skewness, and a five-number summary via QUARTILE.INC along with a histogram of the per-transaction revenue distribution to visualize spending patterns.

title: Cleaning Corrupted POS Data in Excel
text:
7. What I’d Improve

Replace the 9999 sentinel with a value guaranteed never to collide with a real date serial number (see Section 2), or better, use a separate boolean flag column instead of overloading the date field itself to signal validity.
Add a validation flag column that counts how many corrections were applied per row, to make it easy to spot rows that needed unusually heavy cleanup and might warrant a manual look.
The transaction × item incidence matrix (Section 6) is powerful but manual — for a larger item catalog, a proper association-rule approach (support/confidence/lift, as in market-basket analysis) would scale better than reading off a large pivot table by eye.


Course project for K303 (Data Analytics), Kelley School of Business, Indiana University.

title: Coffee Investment Decision Analysis: Power BI & Monte Carlo Simulation
text:
Springfield Beans, a gourmet coffee shop, was approached about purchasing a new crop of specialty Colombian coffee beans, either the full 1-acre harvest or half of it, and had to decide how to structure pre-orders (no deposit, 50% deposit, or 100% deposit) before committing. Both the harvest yield and timing were uncertain, and customer demand depended heavily on how much deposit was required. To tackle this, I split this into two parts:

Explore historical sales data in Power BI to understand demand patterns for whole bean coffee; the closest proxy available for how this new specialty crop might sell.
Build a Monte Carlo simulation in Excel that combined crop yield uncertainty, customer demand uncertainty, and the six possible purchase/deposit decisions into a risk-based recommendation, using the Power BI findings as direct inputs to the simulation.

1. Business Problem
Springfield Beans, a gourmet coffee shop, was approached about purchasing a new crop of specialty Colombian coffee beans, either the full 1-acre harvest or half of it, and had to decide how to structure pre-orders (no deposit, 50% deposit, or 100% deposit) before committing. Both the harvest yield and timing were uncertain, and customer demand depended heavily on how much deposit was required. To tackle this, I split this into two parts:

Explore historical sales data in Power BI to understand demand patterns for whole bean coffee; the closest proxy available for how this new specialty crop might sell.

title: Coffee Investment Decision Analysis: Power BI & Monte Carlo Simulation
section: 2. Part 1 — Power BI: Exploratory & Explanatory Analysis
text:
2. Part 1 — Power BI: Exploratory & Explanatory Analysis
The report is structured as a 5-page navigable dashboard: Home → Overview → Trends → Deep-Dive → Breakdown, with a page-navigator button and hover tooltips on each visual explaining its takeaway and business relevance, built so the report can stand on its own as a presentation, without someone there to narrate it live.



Example of a takeaway on a chart


Visual types used across the report: line charts, pie and donut charts, clustered column and bar charts, a ribbon chart, a pivot table, KPI cards, slicers, and interactive action buttons for navigation.
Key findings driving the investment decision (pulled directly from the report):

Whole bean coffee demand is strongly seasonal, peaking every Q4, with December averaging 391 units — 56% above the monthly average.
The Colombian farm estimated a 50% chance of December delivery (vs. 20% October, 30% November) — meaning the most likely arrival window lines up with the strongest demand period.
Month-specific average and standard deviation of whole bean sales for October, November, and December were calculated directly in Power BI (via grouped queries in Power Query) and fed as the actual input parameters for the off-shelf demand random variables in the Excel simulation — a direct hand-off between the two tools rather than two disconnected analyses.

title: Coffee Investment Decision Analysis: Power BI & Monte Carlo Simulation
text:
3. Part 2 — Excel: Monte Carlo Simulation

Decision Framework
Six decisions were modeled, crossing two choices:




0% Deposit
50% Deposit
100% Deposit




50% of crop
Decision 1
Decision 2
Decision 3


100% of crop
Decision 4
Decision 5
Decision 6





Random Variables

Crop yield: Normal distribution, mean 800 lbs, standard deviation 90 lbs, via NORM.INV(RAND(), mean, stdev).
Orders placed: Binomial distribution over 750 potential customers, using BINOM.INV, with the probability of placing an order depending on deposit level (customers are more willing to place an order with no deposit required — 90% vs. 50% at full deposit).
Orders completed: A second binomial draw, where the probability of actually completing (picking up) a placed order increases with deposit level (70% at no deposit vs. ~100% at full deposit) — modeling the real trade-off between attracting orders and having customers actually follow through.
Harvest-ready month: A discrete random variable (October/November/December) drawn via a cumulative-probability lookup against the farm’s stated delivery odds.
Off-shelf demand: Normal distribution, with mean and standard deviation pulled directly from the Power BI Part 1 analysis, conditioned on whichever month the harvest actually lands in that simulation run.



Simulation Engine
The model uses Excel’s Data Table feature to run 1,000 iterations across all 6 decisions simultaneously, recalculating every random variable each time. Results are summarized on a separate sheet with mean, standard deviation, and the 5th/25th/50th/75th/95th percentiles of profit for every decision — plus P(Profit > $0), giving a direct read on how risky, not just how profitable, each option is.
A “FROZEN” toggle lets a user switch the whole model to deterministic mode (every random variable snaps to its expected value) for sanity-checking the logic, without losing the ability to switch back to full simulation.

Once off-shelf sales of leftover beans are added back in, the picture shifts — the full-crop decisions (4–6) post much higher mean profit (roughly $1,600–$1,900), since off-shelf sales absorb a lot of the excess inventory. But the half-crop decisions still carry dramatically lower risk (P(Profit > $0) of 100% vs. near-zero without the off-shelf boost) — a classic risk vs. expected-value trade-off.
Note on these numbers: because this is a live Monte Carlo simulation (every random variable recalculates on open), the exact figures shift slightly each time the workbook runs. The table above reflects one saved snapshot where the pattern across decisions is the meaningful, stable part, not the specific dollar figures.

title: Coffee Investment Decision Analysis: Power BI & Monte Carlo Simulation
text:
5. Recommendation
From the report: “This data supports investing in the specialty crop. The Excel simulation model recommends Decision 3: half crop, 100% deposit, as the optimal strategy.”
Decision 3 doesn’t post the highest expected profit in every scenario, but it guarantees a positive outcome and the lowest variance of any option, while the highest-expected-value decisions (4–6, without off-shelf sales) carry real risk of a loss. Framing the recommendation around risk tolerance, not just maximizing the average outcome, is the core judgment call of the analysis.

title: Coffee Investment Decision Analysis: Power BI & Monte Carlo Simulation
text:
6. Skills Demonstrated

Power BI: Power Query data transformation, RELATED() calculated columns, Group By aggregation for statistical inputs, custom tooltips, multi-page interactive report design
Excel: Monte Carlo simulation via Data Tables, NORM.INV, BINOM.INV, cumulative-probability lookups for discrete random variables, PERCENTILE.INC risk analysis, dynamic model toggles
Cross-tool integration: using statistical outputs from one tool (Power BI) as calibrated inputs to a second tool’s random variables (Excel) rather than treating the two analyses as siloed deliverables
Decision analysis under uncertainty: framing a recommendation around risk (probability of loss, variance) rather than expected value alone

title: Cleaning Corrupted POS Data in Excel
text:
6. Pivot Table Analysis
With the data cleaned, I used PivotTables to answer a set of specific business questions, each one built on a “scratch” sheet, then the headline answer surfaced onto a clean summary sheet so the underlying pivot mechanics don’t clutter the final report.

Product Analysis








Question
Pivot Table Structure
Answer




What item appears in the most transactions?
Rows: Item → Values: Count of Transaction ID
Pourover


What item was purchased in the largest total quantity?
Rows: Item → Values: Sum of Qty
Pourover (4,144 units)


What food item was purchased in the largest total quantity?
Same as above, filtered to Category = Food
Sticky bun


Which type of whole beans sold in the largest total quantity?
Rows: Item → Values: Sum of Qty, filtered to Type = Whole beans
Single-origin (210 vs. House blend’s 118)



The filtered versions are the more interesting technique here: rather than building a separate pivot from scratch for “food items only” or “whole beans only,” I applied a report filter to the same base structure having the same fields, narrower scope, different question answered.


Trend Analysis








Question
Pivot Table Structure
Answer




What hour does hot drink revenue peak?
Rows: Time (Hour) → Values: Sum of Revenue, filtered to Type = Hot drink
10 AM


What days have the lowest sales for the most popular brewed coffee size?
Rows: Day of the Week → Values: Sum of Qty, filtered to Category = Brewed coffee, Price Point = 12 oz
Monday and Wednesday


Which product type has the most dramatic swing in sales across the week?
Rows: Category × Columns: Day of the Week → Values: Sum of Qty, plus a calculated range column (MAX − MIN across the week)
Hot Drinks (98-unit swing — largest of any category)



That third one is a two-dimensional pivot, a category down the rows, weekday across the columns, with an extra calculated column added alongside the pivot to measure volatility, not just totals. Turning “which category has the most dramatic swing” into a concrete number (rather than eyeballing a table) is the kind of small addition that makes a pivot table answer a sharper question than it can out of the box.


Basket Analysis: A Transaction × Item Incidence Matrix
The most advanced pivot in the workbook answers: “What cold drink item is most often purchased alongside something from the beans category?” (Answer: Frappé.)
Instead of a normal summary pivot, this one uses Rows: Transaction ID, Columns: Item, Values: Count of Category — turning the pivot into a large incidence matrix where each row is one transaction and each column is one item, with a 1 marking “this item was in this transaction.” That structure is what makes co-occurrence analysis possible: it lets you see which items tend to show up in the same transaction as beans purchases, which a simple one-dimensional pivot can’t answer. This is the same basic idea behind real market-basket analysis (“customers who bought X also bought Y”), built here entirely with native PivotTable features rather than a specialized tool.
